MoviePass burned through cash so quickly that it was reportedly forced to take out short-term loans just to keep approving transactions.
sections.today: MoviePass shut down in 2019 after roughly two years of the unlimited offer, having reportedly lost hundreds of millions of dollars, a business school staple example of a subscription price that generated massive user growth while making the company poorer with every new customer it signed up.

takeaway: Explosive user growth isn't good news if each new user actively loses you money.

hook: Survived direct competition from Walmart and Amazon for years, then was killed less by either of them than by its own debt.

sections.origin: Charles Lazarus started as a baby-furniture retailer before pivoting entirely to toys, building Toys R Us into the dominant big-box toy retailer in the US and eventually globally, a household name synonymous with the entire toy-shopping experience for generations of kids.
sections.struggle: In 2005, a group of private equity firms took Toys R Us private in a leveraged buyout, financing the multi-billion-dollar deal largely with debt loaded directly onto the company itself, saddling it with hundreds of millions of dollars a year in interest payments alone, even as Walmart and then Amazon undercut its prices.
sections.turn: That enormous, fixed debt burden left almost no money available for the store renovations, e-commerce investment, or price competitiveness Toys R Us actually needed to fight off online and big-box competition, unlike less-leveraged competitors who had more room to adapt.
sections.today: Toys R Us filed for bankruptcy in 2017 and liquidated its US stores in 2018, and the collapse became a widely cited example of how a leveraged buyout's debt structure, not necessarily the underlying retail business itself, can be the actual cause of a company's death.

takeaway: A healthy-looking business can still be killed by a balance sheet, not just by competitors or changing consumer taste.

hook: Beat Uber to market in India by years, in a category most assumed only a global giant could win.

sections.origin: Bhavish Aggarwal and Ankit Bhati started Ola after Aggarwal had a frustrating experience trying to book a taxi for a road trip, initially aggregating existing taxi operators onto a single booking platform before expanding into a full ride-hailing marketplace with its own driver-partner network.
sections.struggle: Uber entered India in 2013 with deep pockets and global scale, triggering years of an expensive subsidy war for riders and drivers between the two companies, forcing Ola to raise enormous funding rounds just to match Uber's spending and keep drivers from switching platforms.
sections.turn: Ola leaned into features tailored specifically to Indian roads and payment habits, cash payments at a time when card penetration was low, auto-rickshaws as a formal ride category, and broader vehicle-type variety, building deeper on-ground density in smaller Indian cities that Uber was slower to prioritize.
sections.today: Ola remains one of India's two dominant ride-hailing platforms alongside Uber, and later expanded into electric scooters through Ola Electric, taking on the added risk and capital intensity of manufacturing hardware rather than just running a ride marketplace.

takeaway: Being a strong local incumbent with capital of its own can hold off a better-funded global entrant, even without ever fully winning outright.

hook: Turned WhatsApp and Facebook groups into a nationwide retail network of resellers, mostly women, with no inventory of their own.

sections.origin: Vidit Aatrey and Sanjeev Barnwal started Meesho after an earlier idea, an offline daily-deals platform, failed to gain traction. They pivoted to a social commerce model: suppliers list products on the Meesho app, and individual resellers, often homemakers with no capital or storefront, share those catalogs with their own social networks and earn a margin on each sale.
sections.struggle: Convincing sellers with no e-commerce or logistics experience to trust an unfamiliar app-based supply chain, and building a reliable payments and delivery backend for an enormous number of small, geographically scattered resellers, meant solving a far more fragmented operational problem than a typical e-commerce marketplace.
sections.turn: Meesho made listing free for both suppliers and resellers, unlike marketplaces charging commission fees, and focused specifically on smaller Indian towns and cities and price-sensitive shoppers largely ignored by more metro-focused e-commerce platforms, reaching genuinely new online shoppers rather than competing directly for Amazon and Flipkart's existing user base.
sections.today: Meesho became one of India's most widely downloaded shopping apps, credited with bringing a large number of first-time online sellers and buyers, particularly women, into e-commerce through a zero-capital reselling model rather than a traditional storefront.

takeaway: The biggest untapped market can be the people existing platforms aren't designed to include, not the ones they're already fighting over.

hook: Tried to bring the reliability of e-commerce delivery to home services, in a market where finding a trustworthy electrician or cleaner meant asking a neighbor.

sections.origin: Abhiraj Bahal, Raghav Chandra, and Varun Khaitan started Urban Company, originally UrbanClap, as a marketplace connecting customers with local home-service professionals, cleaning, salon services, appliance repair, plumbing, electrical work, aiming to bring standardized pricing and quality assurance to a market that ran almost entirely on word-of-mouth trust.
sections.struggle: Home services required actually training and standardizing a huge, fragmented, largely informal workforce with wildly varying skill levels, while building enough customer trust to book a stranger into their home, a much higher-trust transaction than booking a cab or ordering food.
sections.turn: Urban Company invested heavily in training and certifying its service professionals, standardized tools and product kits, ratings and background verification, and built recurring subscription-style offerings for regular services, treating service quality as a controllable, brand-defining variable rather than leaving it entirely to individual professionals.
sections.today: Urban Company expanded to multiple countries beyond India and remains one of the largest players in organizing India's informal home-services economy into a structured, ratings-driven marketplace, though it has also faced periodic criticism and protests from service professionals over commission structures and working conditions.

takeaway: Standardizing trust in a fragmented service market is a real business, but it means owning quality-control problems a pure listings platform never has to touch.

hook: Built a ride-hailing company around motorbikes, a vehicle type every other major platform treated as an afterthought, and created an entire new transport category in India.

sections.origin: Aravind Sanka, Pavan Guntupalli, and Rishikesh SR started Rapido specifically around bike taxis, betting that Indian cities' traffic congestion made a two-wheeler genuinely faster and cheaper than a car for most short urban trips, a use case Ola and Uber weren't built around.
sections.struggle: Bike taxis operated in a murky regulatory gray zone in much of India, since most state transport regulations weren't written with commercial bike-taxi services in mind, leading to periodic bans, legal challenges, and the need to lobby state by state for clear operating permissions.
sections.turn: Rapido pursued formal regulatory approval city by city and state by state rather than treating the ambiguity as permission to ignore rules entirely, while keeping prices meaningfully below car-based rides and expanding into auto-rickshaws and, eventually, food and parcel delivery using the same two-wheeler fleet.
sections.today: Rapido became the dominant bike-taxi platform in India and has continued expanding its vehicle categories, proving a large, sustainable transport business could be built specifically around the vehicle type India already overwhelmingly used, rather than importing a car-first model built for other markets.

takeaway: The 'obvious' version of a global business model isn't always the right one for a specific local market's actual constraints.

hook: Set out to fix India's meat and seafood supply chain, a category most e-commerce players avoided entirely because of how hard it is to get right.

sections.origin: Abhay Hanjura and Vivek Gupta started Licious after struggling themselves to find consistently fresh, hygienically sourced meat in India, where most meat shopping happened at local unregulated butcher shops with no cold chain and highly inconsistent quality.
sections.struggle: Meat and seafood are about as operationally difficult a category as e-commerce gets: near-zero shelf life, strict cold-chain requirements from farm to doorstep, and a deeply trust-sensitive purchase where a single bad delivery can permanently lose a customer, all in a market with almost no existing organized cold-chain infrastructure to build on.
sections.turn: Licious built its own end-to-end supply chain rather than relying on third-party vendors, controlling sourcing, processing, and cold-chain delivery directly, and invested heavily in food safety certifications and hygiene standards to differentiate clearly from the unregulated local butcher shop experience.
sections.today: Licious became one of India's largest direct-to-consumer meat and seafood brands, a category few investors initially believed could be built at scale in India, by treating supply-chain control as the actual product rather than a background cost to minimize.

takeaway: In categories built on trust and freshness, owning the entire supply chain isn't optional overhead, it's the actual competitive advantage.

hook: Tried to make databases feel as approachable as a spreadsheet, for the huge number of people who needed one but couldn't code.

sections.origin: Howie Liu, Andrew Ofstad, and Emmett Nicholas started Airtable after noticing that powerful relational databases existed but were far too technical for most non-engineers, while spreadsheets, which everyone already knew how to use, weren't built to handle relationships between different types of data well.
sections.struggle: Building a tool flexible enough to replace project trackers, inventory systems, and content calendars all at once, while keeping the interface as simple and familiar-feeling as a spreadsheet, meant solving a genuinely hard product design problem: enormous flexibility without overwhelming complexity for a non-technical user.
sections.turn: Airtable's core innovation was blending a spreadsheet's familiar grid interface with a real relational database underneath, letting non-technical teams link related records, attach files, and build custom views, kanban boards, calendars, without writing any code or understanding database concepts at all.
sections.today: Airtable is used widely by non-technical teams across industries, from content production to operations to CRM-style tracking, as a flexible alternative to either overly rigid enterprise software or overly limited spreadsheets, valued in the billions of dollars.

takeaway: Making powerful technical capability usable by non-technical people is very often a bigger business than making the capability itself more powerful.

hook: Built as an internal tool for a video game that failed, and the leftover chat tool turned out to be worth more than the game ever was.

sections.origin: Stewart Butterfield and his team were building an online game called Glitch, and to coordinate their own small distributed team, they built an internal messaging and file-sharing tool. When Glitch shut down in 2012 after failing to attract enough players, the team realized the internal tool they'd built for themselves was the more interesting product.
sections.struggle: Workplace communication in 2013 was dominated by email and a handful of enterprise chat tools widely disliked for being clunky, and convincing companies to switch their default communication tool, a genuinely habitual, deeply embedded behavior, was a hard sell without an obvious catalyst.
sections.turn: Slack focused obsessively on making workplace chat feel fast, searchable, and even fun, integrations with other tools, customizable notifications, a friendly tone, treating internal software with the same design care usually reserved for consumer apps, and grew largely through word-of-mouth adoption inside individual teams before spreading company-wide.
sections.today: Slack became one of the defining workplace communication tools of the 2010s, and Salesforce acquired it in 2021 for around $27.7 billion, a striking outcome for a chat tool that began as a side effect of a video game nobody ended up playing.

takeaway: The thing you build to solve your own team's problem while working on something else can turn out to be the actual business.

hook: Built as voice chat for gamers, then quietly became one of the largest general-purpose community platforms on the internet.

sections.origin: Jason Citron and Stan Vishnevskiy had previously built a gaming studio and a game that didn't take off before pivoting to solve a problem they'd experienced directly: existing voice-chat tools for gamers were unreliable and clunky, so they built Discord specifically for low-latency voice communication during gameplay.
sections.struggle: The voice and text chat space already had established players, and gamers are a notoriously specific, hard-to-win-over audience with strong existing habits around whichever tool their friend group already used, making initial adoption dependent almost entirely on organic word-of-mouth within gaming communities rather than paid marketing.
sections.turn: Discord made servers easy to create and free to use with strong voice quality and low latency, building deep loyalty within gaming communities first, then found that its core structure, persistent topic-based text and voice channels for a community, generalized naturally well beyond gaming into hobbyist groups, study groups, and even professional communities during the pandemic.
sections.today: Discord grew into a platform used by hundreds of millions of people well beyond its original gaming audience, and its own path, from a niche utility for a specific hobby into broad general-purpose infrastructure, closely mirrors how several other major consumer platforms found their eventual mainstream audience.

takeaway: Solving a niche audience's specific pain point extremely well is often the fastest path to a much larger audience later.

hook: Made stock trading free for everyone, and forced the entire brokerage industry to follow within a matter of months.

sections.origin: Vlad Tenev and Baiju Bhatt, former Stanford roommates who had built high-frequency trading software for financial institutions, started Robinhood on the observation that the technology cost of executing a trade was minimal, yet retail brokerages still charged customers several dollars in commission per trade, a fee that mainly priced out smaller investors.
sections.struggle: Traditional brokerages made significant revenue from those per-trade commissions, so undercutting them entirely to zero meant Robinhood needed an alternative revenue model, and building a regulated brokerage from scratch required navigating extensive financial compliance requirements as a young startup with no track record.
sections.turn: Robinhood eliminated trading commissions entirely, monetizing instead through payment for order flow, routing trades through market makers who pay for that flow, and other services, and built a simple, mobile-first, gamified interface that appealed strongly to a new generation of first-time retail investors who found traditional brokerage platforms intimidating.
sections.today: Robinhood's zero-commission model forced nearly every major traditional brokerage to eliminate trading fees within about a year, reshaping the entire industry's economics, though the company has also faced scrutiny, including during the 2021 GameStop trading frenzy, over conflicts of interest in its order-flow revenue model and periods of platform instability during high-volume trading.

takeaway: Undercutting an entire industry's pricing model can win a market fast, but it also means the whole industry immediately copies your move.

hook: Made 'buy now, pay later' a mainstream checkout option, turning installment payments into standard e-commerce infrastructure rather than something reserved for big-ticket purchases.

sections.origin: Sebastian Siemiatkowski, Niklas Adalberth, and Victor Jacobsson started Klarna in Sweden focused on making online payments feel safer and simpler for both shoppers and merchants, initially letting customers receive goods before paying for them, reducing the risk shoppers felt buying from unfamiliar online stores.
sections.struggle: Convincing merchants to accept a new payment method meant proving Klarna could reduce fraud and payment risk better than existing card processors, while regulators in different countries had varying, evolving rules around consumer credit that a pan-European, later global, payments company had to navigate country by country.
sections.turn: Klarna expanded its core installment idea into 'buy now, pay later' as a distinct checkout option, letting customers split purchases into several interest-free installments integrated directly into merchant checkouts, and partnered with a huge number of online retailers, turning what once felt like a niche credit product into an ordinary checkout button.
sections.today: Klarna became one of Europe's most valuable fintech startups and a major global player in the buy-now-pay-later category, though the sector as a whole has drawn increasing regulatory scrutiny over concerns about consumers accumulating debt across multiple BNPL providers simultaneously.

takeaway: Turning a financial product into a single checkout button can drive massive adoption, but it can also make debt too frictionless.

hook: A Swiss engineer studied burrs stuck to his dog's fur under a microscope, and turned the tiny hooks he saw into one of the most versatile fasteners ever made.

sections.origin: George de Mestral, a Swiss electrical engineer, went on a hunting trip in the 1940s and noticed burrs from burdock plants clinging stubbornly to his clothes and his dog's fur. Curious, he examined a burr under a microscope and found it covered in tiny hooks that caught on anything with a loop-like surface, including fabric and fur.
sections.struggle: Replicating that natural hook-and-loop mechanism in a manufacturable fabric took de Mestral years of experimentation, initially with cotton, which wore out too quickly, before he found that nylon, when sewn under infrared light, formed durable hooks that could be manufactured reliably and cheaply at scale.
sections.turn: De Mestral patented the invention in 1955, naming it Velcro, a blend of the French words velours (velvet) and crochet (hook), and the fastener found its first major adoption through NASA's space program, used to secure objects in zero gravity, before spreading into everyday clothing, shoes, and countless other products.
sections.today: Velcro became a generic shorthand term for hook-and-loop fasteners broadly, much to the actual Velcro company's ongoing trademark-protection frustration, used in everything from children's shoes to medical devices to spacecraft, all traced back to one engineer's curiosity about burrs stuck to his dog.

takeaway: Nature has already solved an enormous number of engineering problems, sometimes inventing something new just means noticing an existing solution closely enough.

hook: A father-son team discovered a breakthrough waterproof fabric almost by accident, by yanking a heated rod of plastic as hard as they could out of frustration.

sections.origin: Wilbert 'Bill' Gore left DuPont to start his own company experimenting with PTFE, the material behind Teflon, for wire insulation and other applications, working alongside his son Bob Gore, who continued experimenting with ways to stretch the material further without breaking it.
sections.struggle: Standard slow stretching of heated PTFE kept causing it to snap or fail to expand into a usable material, and years of methodical experimentation with different heating and stretching techniques hadn't produced the breakthrough Bob Gore was looking for.
sections.turn: In 1969, in a moment of frustration after repeated failed attempts, Bob Gore yanked a heated rod of PTFE abruptly and forcefully instead of stretching it slowly and evenly, and it expanded successfully into a strong, porous membrane, expanded PTFE, that was windproof and waterproof yet breathable enough to let water vapor escape, exactly the combination outdoor gear had never achieved before.
sections.today: Gore-Tex became the standard waterproof-breathable membrane used across outdoor and performance clothing worldwide, and W.L. Gore & Associates remains privately held with an unusually flat management structure, no traditional titles or hierarchy, that the company credits directly with fostering the kind of experimentation that led to the discovery.

takeaway: Sometimes the breakthrough comes from breaking the careful process you'd been following, not from following it more precisely.

hook: A Hungarian architecture professor built a 3D puzzle to teach his students about structural movement, and it took him a month to solve his own invention.

sections.origin: Ernő Rubik, a professor of architecture in Budapest, built the first prototype cube as a teaching tool to help his students visualize three-dimensional structural movement, designing an interlocking mechanism that let each face rotate independently without the whole cube falling apart.
sections.struggle: After building the mechanism, Rubik scrambled it to test whether it worked, and then realized he had no idea how to restore it to its original solved state, reportedly taking him about a month of his own effort to figure out a method to solve it, before he'd even considered it as a commercial product.
sections.turn: Rubik patented the design and it was licensed for wider Hungarian production in the late 1970s under communist Hungary's limited export system, before an international licensing deal in 1980 brought it to global toy shelves as the Rubik's Cube, arriving at exactly the right moment to become a defining fad of the decade.
sections.today: The Rubik's Cube became one of the best-selling toys in history, and speedcubing, competitively solving it as fast as possible, remains an active global subculture and competitive sport decades after its invention, still built around the same underlying mechanism Rubik designed to teach a geometry lesson.

takeaway: Sometimes the most successful products come from solving a much smaller, more specific problem than the one that eventually makes them famous.

hook: Invented from a gunky residue that kept clogging up oil rigs, which workers were already smearing on cuts and burns before anyone sold it as a product.

sections.origin: Robert Chesebrough, a chemist, visited Pennsylvania oil fields in the 1850s and noticed rig workers had been informally using a paraffin-like residue called 'rod wax,' a gunk that built up on drilling equipment, to soothe cuts, burns, and dry skin, well before anyone had refined or sold it as anything.
sections.struggle: Chesebrough had to figure out how to extract and purify the useful petroleum jelly from the raw, dark, tar-like residue, considered an industrial nuisance by oil drillers, into a clean, stable, colorless product safe and appealing enough for people to actually want to put on their skin.
sections.turn: After refining the process, Chesebrough spent years personally demonstrating the product's healing properties, reportedly burning and cutting his own skin in public demonstrations and applying the jelly to show it worked, to convince skeptical audiences and pharmacists to stock what he named Vaseline.
sections.today: Vaseline remains one of the most recognized skincare brands in the world, still sold in a form very close to Chesebrough's original refined petroleum jelly, a product built entirely out of what oil drillers originally considered waste.

takeaway: An industrial byproduct nobody wants can be worth more than the intended product, if someone bothers to find out what it's actually good for.

hook: A naval engineer accidentally knocked a tension spring off a shelf, watched it 'walk' across the floor, and a toy company was born.

sections.origin: Richard James, a naval engineer, was working on tension springs designed to stabilize sensitive equipment on ships during World War II. He accidentally knocked one of his prototype springs off a shelf and watched it 'walk' end over end down a stack of books, onto a table, and onto the floor, rather than simply falling.
sections.struggle: James recognized the walking motion was oddly captivating but had no obvious commercial purpose as a toy yet, and needed to find the right gauge of steel and coil tension that would walk reliably and durably, essentially reverse-engineering an accident into a repeatable product with no engineering application driving the design anymore.
sections.turn: His wife, Betty James, found the name 'Slinky' in a dictionary, meaning stealthy and graceful, and the couple demonstrated the toy at Gimbels department store in Philadelphia in 1945, selling their entire initial stock within about 90 minutes once shoppers saw it walk down an inclined board in person.
sections.today: The Slinky has sold hundreds of millions of units since its 1945 launch and remains a recognizable toy today, a rare case where the entire product concept came directly from watching an engineering failure fall off a shelf the right way.

takeaway: An accident is only useless until someone stops to ask why it happened to do something interesting.
